The structural problems in Medicare Advantage are well documented, and they compound on each other.

Start with the money. CBO's most recent baseline puts Medicare Advantage overpayments at roughly $1 trillion over the next decade, driven by a beneficiary switching from traditional Medicare to MA costing the federal government about 15 percent more on average. MedPAC's 2026 estimate is $76 billion for this year alone, 14 percent above the same beneficiaries' cost in fee for service Medicare. The Senate Joint Economic Committee traced these overpayments to Part B premiums directly, adding $212 per beneficiary in 2025 alone, a cost borne by everyone on Medicare, including those never enrolled in MA.

The excess payment is not evidence the underlying model cannot work. MedPAC's own Chapter 11 status report data show MA cost more than traditional Medicare in nearly every year from 2007 through 2014 even before coding intensity and favorable selection are counted, but that baseline gap has narrowed toward zero and turned negative in several recent years once those two effects are stripped out. The distortion is concentrated in gaming layered on the program, not the model itself, and that gaming does not yet include quality bonus spending, which sits on top of both.

This all matters for independent practices because Medicare runs under budget neutrality. Dollars flowing to MA overpayments and quality bonuses are dollars unavailable for fee schedule updates. Independent practices absorb the fallout of a payment fight they are not even engaged in.

Network dynamics compound it. UnitedHealthcare has significantly narrowed its Medicare Advantage networks across multiple markets in 2026, citing elevated medical loss ratios. Becker's Hospital Review has tracked more than two dozen health systems terminating MA contracts with major insurers this year, most citing prior authorization denials and slow reimbursement, including Mayo Clinic and Brown University Health.

Vertical integration adds another layer. When an insurer also owns the largest physician employment network in the country, independent practices are negotiating against a counterparty that profits from steering patients toward its own employed physicians. Georgetown's CHIR research confirms this is not just a theory. The same insurer pays its own employed physicians more than independent physicians for identical services.

None of this reflects a program broken beyond repair. It reflects specific, identifiable mechanisms, coding intensity, favorable selection, and an unaccountable bonus program, layered onto a delivery model MedPAC's own data suggest could otherwise be cost competitive with traditional Medicare. The system is performing exactly as it was designed.

Lawsuit Claims UnitedHealth AI Denied Elderly Care with 90% Error Rate
A class-action suit in Minnesota federal court accuses UnitedHealth of using the nH Predict AI tool, with a claimed 90% error rate, to deny post-acute care to Medicare Advantage patients like Lokken. The company denies the tool drives decisions, insisting physicians make final calls while approving 98% of eligible claims overall; only 0.2% of patients appeal, though over 90% of those denials reverse. Public posts share personal denial stories and images linking to the case and the 2024 killing of CEO Brian Thompson, amid reports of doubled denial rates post-tool rollout and an ongoing Senate probe. The court has ordered more records on the tool as discovery proceeds.

This week I want to spend some time on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage and what it means for independent physician practices and their patients.

Medicare Advantage now covers nearly 55% of all Medicare beneficiaries. 99% of those enrollees are subject to prior authorization requirements for at least some services. In 2024, Medicare Advantage plans denied 4.1 million prior authorization requests, a 56% increase over recent years. 81% of those denials were overturned on appeal. Only 11.5% of patients ever appealed.

That gap between the overturn rate and the appeal rate tells you everything you need to know about how this system functions in practice. It is built on the reasonable expectation that most patients and physicians will not have the time or resources to fight back.

This week I will cover the scale of the burden on independent practices, the growing role of artificial intelligence in denial decisions, the documented patient harm that has resulted, and the legislative solutions that are currently on the table.

Medicare Just Shrank. Millions Will Get This Wrong (Part D 2027) A letter could be sitting in your mailbox right now saying the hospital you've trusted for years won't take your insurance anymore. In 2026, roughly 25 of America's biggest hospital systems; Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, even the system half of New York depends on: dropped or narrowed Medicare Advantage. And there's one mistake seniors make when switching that can lock them out for life.
I'm Neal K. Shah, a Johns Hopkins- and NIH-funded caregiving researcher and CEO of CareYaya, and I've helped thousands of families navigate aging, dementia, and insurance denials. Here I break down what's happening to Medicare Advantage right now, why hospitals are walking away, and the five moves that can keep a family from losing their doctor and their savings. If you or someone you love is on Medicare Advantage, this one's for you.  More than half of America's seniors are on Medicare Advantage and by one estimate, nearly 3 million were forced to change plans for 2026 after their plan pulled out, shrank, or cut benefits.

Last night, I got off the phone with a family member in New Jersey who is dealing with cancer.

Their doctor ordered an imaging study.

Their insurance company denied it.

Think about how insane that sentence is.

A physician treating a patient with cancer determined that imaging was medically necessary and somewhere between that examination room and the scanner, an insurance company decided otherwise.

After we hung up, I couldn’t stop thinking about it.

So I started reading.

And reading.

And digging through the numbers.

I wanted to understand how we got to a place where someone can have a doctor say, “You need this,” and still have to convince an insurance company that their doctor is right.

What I found pissed me off even more.

America does not have a healthcare spending problem.

America has a healthcare accountability problem.

On May 28, 2026, a major international comparison of 20 countries found that the United States spends MORE on healthcare than any country studied.

18% of our entire GDP.

Nearly TWICE the OECD average.

And what do we get for it?

Americans still die younger.

Our life expectancy is nearly FIVE YEARS shorter than Japan, Spain, and Switzerland.

We are more likely to skip medically necessary care because we cannot afford it.

And while patients are trying to stay alive, insurance companies are still deciding whether the treatment their DOCTOR ordered is “medically necessary.”

In 2024 alone, Medicare Advantage insurers denied 4.1 MILLION prior-authorization requests.

Here is the part that should make your blood boil:

When those denials were appealed, more than 80% were overturned.

So I have a proposal.

If an insurance company overrules my physician, I want the name of the person who made that decision.

Their medical degree.

Their specialty.

Their license number.

And their signature.

No hiding behind “internal policy.”

No hiding behind “utilization management.”

No anonymous committee.

If you have the authority to tell a cancer patient they cannot have a scan…

tell a chronic pain patient they cannot have medication…

tell a disabled person they cannot have therapy…

or force someone who is already sick to fight an insurance company for treatment their doctor says they need…

PUT YOUR NAME ON THE DENIAL.

Because this is not a spreadsheet.

This is someone’s mother.

Someone’s father.

Someone’s child.

Someone’s life.

We spend more than everybody else.

Patients ration care.

Doctors drown in paperwork.

And corporations call it efficiency.

Enough.

Healthcare does not exist to protect an insurance company’s bottom line.

Insurance exists to pay for healthcare.

We have somehow allowed those two things to become reversed.

Put patients back in the center of medicine.

Put physicians back in charge of medical decisions.

And if you are going to stand between a sick human being and the care their doctor prescribed,

have the courage to put your fucking name on it.

PUT YOUR NAME ON THE DENIAL.

A private insurer just decided that a cancer patient could not have her chemotherapy in the cancer center. She walked away from treatment entirely. This is the rollout most clinicians have not noticed yet, and it is starting in rural America by design.
 
Banu Symington has practiced hematology-oncology in highly rural settings for more than 20 years. In May, at a state oncology meeting, the room was told three things were "coming down the pike": white bagging, brown bagging, and off-site infusions. They were framed as remote possibilities.
 
Within a week, two of her insurance carriers sent her letters. They would no longer reimburse chemotherapy delivered inside the cancer center. She was to write orders sending her patients to an independent infusion suite owned by a community pharmacist, staffed only by nurses, with no oncologist on the floor, no nurse practitioner trained to manage an infusion reaction, no ER down the hall, no code blue team in the building. Infusion reactions can occur at any cycle, not just the first.
 
She appealed. The insurer denied the appeal. Her hospital's finance manager offered to match the off-site price so the chemotherapy could remain in a setting where a physician could intervene. The insurer refused to negotiate.
 
One of her patients withdrew from chemotherapy entirely. She would not go off-site, and she could not pay out of pocket. So the treatment ended.
 
The strategy is rural-first by design. Fewer rural physicians, fewer rural patients, less organized resistance. Once it scales there, urban centers are next. Medicare is not doing this. Private insurance is. Medicare Advantage, which is private insurance administering Medicare, is beginning to.
 
Save the framework, three rollout vectors to watch in your market:
1. Off-site infusion mandates: chemotherapy moved out of the cancer center to an unsupervised, for-profit suite
2. White bagging: drugs shipped to the hospital pharmacy with no margin retained, eroding the only line that keeps rural cancer centers solvent
3. Brown bagging: cytotoxic drugs shipped directly to the patient's home, then carried in, with no chain-of-custody guarantee on temperature or handling
 
Cancer centers do not break even on Medicare or Medicaid. The small margin on privately insured patients is what keeps them open. Strip that margin and the centers close. The patients then drive further, or stop.

A Medicare Advantage insurer can leave a county. The senior cannot leave the consequences.

UnitedHealthcare entered 2026 expecting to lose more than 1.1 million Medicare Advantage members after reducing its footprint to restore margins. Elevance, CVS, Centene, and other large insurers also shed members.

Humana took the other side of the trade. It kept more generous benefits in its remaining markets and attracted more than one million new seniors. It may finish 2026 as the country’s largest Medicare Advantage insurer.

Now Humana says it will exit more plans in 2027 to improve profitability.

This tells us something important about where the program places volatility.

Insurers expand when benchmarks, risk adjustment, star ratings, and utilization produce attractive economics. When those economics deteriorate, they reduce benefits, narrow networks, close plans, or leave markets.

That may make financial sense for the insurer. It creates real disruption for everyone else.

A senior must select new coverage, identify which physicians remain in-network, compare drug formularies, and start over with a new set of benefits.

The physician’s office must verify the coverage, learn another authorization system, resolve interrupted treatment, renegotiate contracts, and clean up denied claims.

Medicare Advantage promises coordinated care. Coordination requires stability.

A plan that disappears whenever its margin disappoints never absorbs the full cost of its own exit. It distributes that cost across seniors, families, physicians, pharmacies, and the rest of the delivery system.

For all of the we’re trying crew….

Here’s What CMS and the Executive Branch Could Do Tomorrow Without Congress

a concrete list of actions CMS and HHS can take under existing authority. No bills. No committees. No “we tried.” These are decisions — and they’re all sitting on some bought off administrators desk.

1. Expand site-neutral payments.
Stop paying hospital-owned clinics more for the same service. It’s the single biggest driver of consolidation, and CMS can fix it with a pen.

2. Restrict anti-competitive physician non-competes.
CMS can condition Medicare/MA participation on fair employment terms instead of letting systems trap physicians and patients inside corporate fences.

3. Rein in prior authorization abuse.
Gold-carding, real timelines, specialty-matched reviewers, penalties for bad-faith denials — all possible now, without Congress.

4. Force Medicare Advantage transparency.
Publish denial rates, appeals, overturns, steering patterns, and utilization rules. MA has gotten away with too much because no one forces sunlight.

5. Fix Stark enforcement so it stops crushing small practices.
Clarify exceptions, stop weaponizing technical violations, and rewrite guidance that only massive systems can navigate.

6. Update practice-expense RVUs to reflect reality.
CMS controls RVU inputs. Adjusting them to match real private-practice overhead would stabilize half the physician economy.

7. Expand ASC and office-based procedure lists.
More spine, ortho, neuro, pain. Safer, cheaper, faster access. No legislative barrier.

8. Reform the audit and recoupment circus.
End extrapolated audits below defined thresholds. Require specialist reviewers. Fix recoupment timelines so small practices aren’t bankrupted by process.

9. Reduce the MIPS/MACRA administrative tax.
Simplify measures. Cut redundant documentation. Expand exemptions. CMS can do all of this with rulemaking.

10. Strengthen MA network adequacy.
Stop allowing MA plans to wall off independent physicians. Enforce real access standards and real specialist availability.

11. Expand telehealth flexibilities.
Fix originating-site rules, clean up supervision requirements, modernize modalities — low-hanging fruit.

12. Clean up enrollment and revalidation.
PECOS, site visits, and redundant documentation are pure administrative friction. CMS created these headaches; CMS can remove them.

13. Create physician-led models through CMMI (I hate CMMI, but if we’re going to spend money on it, this is the one good use of it.)
Independent specialist bundles, physician-led ACOs, and competition-friendly payment models are all within CMMI’s administrative authority.

14. Tackle corporate vertical integration that hides behind federal rules.
CMS can audit “steering,” offloading, and self-preferencing inside vertically integrated systems. They simply choose not to.

15. Enforce competitive fairness as a condition of Medicare participation.
CMS could take a harder stance on anti-competitive contracting, referral capture, and network manipulation — today.

Despite what you’re told about healthcare, a lot of the changes that would actually improve physician standing, improve access, and strengthen independent practices don’t require a single act of Congress. 

People keep pretending that everything hinges on some giant bipartisan bill. It doesn’t. Yes, unwinding the ACA and fixing the statutory mess is a legislative priority, and yes, there are structural problems only Congress can solve. 

But the day-to-day realities that crush private practice — the regulatory burdens, the anti-competitive advantages given to hospitals, the games Medicare Advantage plays, the audits, the prior authorization hurdles, the facility-fee distortions, the non-competes — those are almost entirely executive-branch problems. They can be fixed tomorrow.

That’s my frustration with both parties. We keep hearing, “Well, we need legislation.” No, you don’t. Stop lying. Stop using Congress as the excuse for why nothing changes. 

There are dozens of meaningful, practical actions CMS and HHS can take right now under existing authority. And these aren’t minor tweaks. They directly affect whether independent physicians survive. They directly affect whether patients can actually see a doctor without waiting months. They directly affect whether every year gets harder and more expensive for small practices to operate.

People think improving physician standing is only about raising reimbursement. It’s not. In private practice, costs matter just as much — regulatory overhead, compliance burden, administrative requirements, audits, prior auth, MA games, Stark ambiguity, enrollment hassle, and the facility-fee bias. Every year I’m paid less. Every year my costs go up. Every year the regulatory demands multiply. If CMS and the Executive Branch simply cut the regulatory weight they themselves created, that alone would be a major win. But they don’t.

So when Republicans or Democrats or anyone in any party says, “We’ve tried,” my response is simple: no, you haven’t. You haven’t even scratched the surface of what you could do without Congress. There is a long list of actions that could materially improve life for physicians and patients tomorrow. And none of them require a 2,000-page bill. They require a decision.

Continuing this week's focus on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage, today I want to look at what the data actually shows about the burden on independent physician practices.

The Medical Group Management Association's Regulatory Burden Report found that 97% of providers have experienced delays or denials for medically necessary care due to prior authorization requirements. For independent practices, this burden is not absorbed by a large administrative infrastructure. It falls on physicians, nurses, and front office staff who are already stretched thin.

Physicians in independent practice describe a cyclical pattern of denial. The same treatment plans are challenged repeatedly. Peer-to-peer reviews consume clinical time without consistent outcomes and typically without a real peer. Standards vary from insurer to insurer and even plan to plan within the same insurer frustrating physicians trying to navigate the gauntlet of varied protocols.

Against that backdrop, the health insurance industry announced a voluntary commitment earlier this year to reduce prior authorization volume by 11% in 2026, benchmarked against 2024 claim volume. That is the same period in which Medicare Advantage denial rates had increased 56%! 

The American Medical Group Association, which represents 400 medical groups, called it "barely scratching the surface" and noted that the reduction does not apply to prescription drug prior authorizations at all, which many physicians identify as their most significant daily burden.

One retinal specialist was direct about what meaningful reform requires: if insurers want credit for change, they need to be transparent enough for independent verification. Voluntary pledges with aggregate numbers that cannot be audited at the CPT code level are not accountability.

Independent practices cannot sustain this. The administrative cost is real, and it ultimately comes at the expense of patient care.

On July 6, WISeR's gold-carding exemption went live. To qualify, a physician needs at least 10 prior authorization submissions and a 90 percent affirmation rate during the assessment period. Physicians who clear that bar are exempted entirely from prior authorization and pre-payment review on WISeR-covered services for a defined period, subject to periodic re-evaluation. Cohere Health, the model participant for Texas, has told the Texas Medical Association that gold-carded claims will be automatically identified and pushed through without manual review.

Gold carding has been a physician ask for years, and until now it has existed mainly at the state level. Texas passed its own gold-card law for state-regulated plans in 2021 and amended it in 2025. No Medicare Advantage plan has built a comparable federal exemption pathway for physicians with strong track records. WISeR did it in just six months.

The early data is not clean. Reporting on Texas found initial prior authorization approval rates running around 62 percent, rising to 84 percent after peer-to-peer review, lower than approval rates typically reported in Medicare Advantage, though those figures reflect a single state in a limited early window. There have been real technical problems with contractor portals, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation has an open Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against CMS seeking more detail on the AI tools model participants use. Those are legitimate accountability questions that CMS will need to answer in full.

That being said, the honest comparison is not WISeR against a perfect system. It is WISeR against the Medicare Advantage prior authorization physicians already live with, where initial denials are overturned on appeal at strikingly high rates, contractors carry no gold-card obligation at all, and physicians frequently cannot get a real peer-to-peer review with a same-specialty clinician. Measured against that baseline, WISeR's early numbers are a starting point for improvement, not a reason to scrap a model that is structurally built better than the alternative.

Today I want to focus on the human side of the prior authorization data we have been discussing this week.

On February 11, 2026, the Senate Special Committee on Aging convened a hearing titled "The Doctor is Out: How Washington's Rules Drove Physicians Out of Medicine." Prior authorization was a central topic. Members of both parties and every witness who testified agreed that administrative burden, with prior authorization at the top of the list, is a primary driver of physician burnout and a direct threat to the quality of patient care.

The underlying data supports that conclusion. 89% of physicians report that prior authorization often or sometimes leads to delays in patient care. More than one in four physicians say that a prior authorization issue led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care, including hospitalization or permanent damage. A federal investigation by the Department of Health and Human Services found that 13% of Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials were for requests that actually met Medicare's own coverage criteria.

For independent practices, this is not an abstract policy problem. These are physicians who have treated the same patients for years, sometimes for decades. When a prior authorization delay holds up a cancer treatment, a surgical procedure, or a skilled nursing placement, the physician on the other end of that denial knows exactly what it means for that specific patient. The peer-to-peer review that follows takes that physician out of the exam room, away from other patients, to argue for care that should not require an argument.

Every hour spent on prior authorization administration is an hour that does not go to patient care. Every denial that goes unchallenged because a small practice cannot absorb another round of appeals represents a patient who received less care than they were entitled to.

Tomorrow I will outline the specific legislative steps that can address this. The February Senate hearing demonstrated genuine bipartisan interest in reform. The policy solutions exist. What has been missing is the will to move them forward.

Just a reminder…
While everyone waits on Congress, a hard truth keeps being ignored. 

Much of what is broken in U.S. healthcare persists because CMS and HHS refuse to fully use the authority they already have. 

These are not legislative fantasies. 

They are administrative decisions that can be implemented through rulemaking, contracting, and enforcement. Where statute limits action, CMS should say so plainly instead of hiding behind inertia.

First, expand site-neutral payments wherever statutory flexibility exists. CMS can continue narrowing unjustified payment differentials between hospital-owned clinics and independent practices. Full site-neutrality may require Congress, but meaningful progress does not.

Second, address physician non-competes through Medicare participation and access standards where legally defensible. CMS cannot rewrite state contract law, but it can stop tolerating employment practices that restrict patient choice and physician mobility.

Third, rein in prior authorization abuse in Medicare Advantage. CMS already regulates MA operations and can enforce real timelines, specialty-matched reviewers, and consequences for bad-faith denials. Weak enforcement is a choice.

Fourth, restore and expand Medicare Advantage transparency. CMS has authority to require reporting of denial rates, appeals, overturns, utilization controls, and steering behavior. Pausing transparency reflects policy preference, not lack of power.

Fifth, modernize Stark enforcement. Stark is statutory, but CMS controls guidance and enforcement posture. Technical foot-faults should not function as a consolidation weapon that only large systems can survive.

Sixth, update practice-expense RVUs to reflect real private-practice overhead. Budget neutrality constrains totals, but CMS controls methodology and can stop systematically disadvantaging independent practices.

Seventh, aggressively expand ASC and office-based procedure lists. CMS has clear authority to add procedures through rulemaking. More spine, ortho, neuro, and pain care can safely move out of hospitals with lower cost and better access.

Eighth, reform audits and recoupment. CMS controls contractor behavior, extrapolation thresholds, reviewer qualifications, and timelines. Small practices should not be bankrupted by process alone.

Ninth, reduce the MIPS and MACRA administrative burden. CMS cannot eliminate MACRA, but it can simplify measures, cut redundant documentation, and broaden exemptions.

Tenth, enforce real Medicare Advantage network adequacy. CMS already sets standards and can penalize plans that exclude independent physicians while claiming adequate access.

Eleventh, expand telehealth flexibilities where CMS retains authority, including supervision, documentation, coding, and modality rules.

Twelfth, clean up enrollment and revalidation. PECOS dysfunction and redundant site visits are administrative creations that CMS can fix.

Thirteenth, prioritize physician-led models through CMMI. Independent bundles and physician-led ACOs are well within CMMI’s authority and would introduce real competition.

Fourteenth, expose and penalize steering and self-preferencing inside vertically integrated Medicare Advantage organizations and refer anticompetitive conduct to DOJ and FTC.

Fifteenth, enforce competitive fairness through existing Medicare participation standards tied to access, nondiscrimination, and payment integrity.

This is not about pretending CMS can rewrite statutes overnight. Consolidation, access shortages, and physician attrition were engineered by payment rules, weak enforcement, opaque Medicare Advantage behavior, and an administrative tax that punishes independence. CMS and HHS already control many of those levers. Continued inaction is not bureaucratic. It is deliberate.

Something underhanded is happening inside Medicare and Medicaid, and no one’s talking about it, but it’s about to change how millions get treated.
An oncologist I spoke with recently told me something that stopped me cold. Starting next year, she said, every cancer treatment she prescribes for patients on Medicare Advantage or Medicaid will require prior approval. Not just for experimental therapies or risky procedures—everything. Even the routine. The decisions are no longer hers to make. They’re deferred to remote systems, reviewed by people she’s never met, many of whom may not be physicians at all.
She didn’t use the term, but what she described sounded eerily close to what critics once called death panels. It’s probably too strong a phrase. Still, it captures something about the shift underway: the way life-preserving care is now filtered through layers of authorization, delay, and denial. None of it is accountable to the patient.
We’ve been told that privatizing Medicare would lead to innovation, flexibility, and smarter use of resources. It’s a story that’s been repeated long enough to sound like common sense. But for patients navigating serious illness, especially those living on fixed incomes, the promises vanish the moment treatment is needed. Beginning January 1, 2026, a new set of policies will require physicians treating cancer patients under Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care to submit for prior approval before delivering care that used to be routine. These changes aren’t theoretical—they’re already being implemented and modeled in anticipation.
What was once a matter of clinical judgment between doctor and patient is being rerouted through an administrative gauntlet. Treatment plans will be paused while paperwork moves through opaque systems. Approvals that used to be immediate will be delayed. Appeals may stretch out over days or weeks. This isn’t about rare procedures or experimental therapies. The requirements will extend to standard care. The review won’t be performed by someone with direct knowledge of the patient—or necessarily by a physician at all. The rationale won’t be medical. It will be financial.
Delay isn’t a side effect. It’s the strategy. Every treatment deferred, every procedure denied, becomes a line of surplus in a system where profit is made not by healing, but by avoiding the cost of it. The fewer approvals processed, the more money retained. These are not decisions shaped by care. They are decisions shaped by silence—by hesitation, by distance, by the absence of resistance.
This is how rationing works in a privatized state. Not through force. Through systems. Through thresholds that move. Through policies that sound reasonable until you need them to respond. And when they don’t, there’s no one to appeal to. The system isn’t broken. It’s sealed.
For those enrolled in Medicare Advantage—plans marketed as more efficient, more integrated, more modern—this is the tradeoff. Lower up-front costs come at the price of discretion. You may no longer be free to act on your doctor’s recommendation without additional steps. Those steps aren’t about safety. They’re about managing expenditures in a system that rewards denial.
This isn’t just a bureaucratic failure. It’s the cultural reengineering of care. What was once an ethic of shared protection has been repackaged as managed risk. The patient becomes a cost center. Illness becomes a data point. Survival is now negotiated—case by case, code by code.
The consequences are not evenly distributed. They follow the same lines they always have—income, geography, race, insurance class. What presents as efficiency is more often a gatekeeping device. Those already on the margins are the first to wait. The last to be approved. The easiest to disappear into the backlog.
This is power not in its spectacular form, but in its administrative mode—the kind that decides who waits and who moves forward, who receives care as a right and who receives it as a favor. It governs not by issuing decrees, but by deciding which lives can afford to be delayed. This is how life is managed, and death is administered—not by violence, but by withdrawal.
From a political ecology perspective, this is a system designed to manage vulnerability, not by addressing it, but by distributing it. It governs not through direct care, but through selective abandonment, allocating life chances through a logic of scarcity. What gets called efficiency is often just rationing by another name.
From an anthropological perspective, these systems don’t impose power from above. They embed it in routine. They normalize it through repetition. Waiting, in this context, becomes a tool of governance—an ordinary mechanism for deciding who can afford to endure delay and who cannot. It is a slow, administrative form of violence, harder to detect than force, but no less consequential.
Some argue these policies are necessary to contain costs in an aging society. But cost containment isn’t neutral. It always lands hardest on those with the least time and the fewest resources. While administrators speak of oversight and sustainability, patients are left to wait. Sometimes too long.
This wasn’t the promise of Medicare. It was supposed to be a bulwark—a collective safeguard against the precarity of aging and illness. Medicare Advantage has reframed that promise through market logic. What began as a public good is now filtered through private incentives. What was once a guarantee is now a margin call.
These aren’t simply budget decisions. They’re life decisions, managed through process. A quiet calculus unfolds in the background—who gets to live well, and who can be left to linger in the queue.
This is what happens when governance is reorganized around cost rather than care—when what we call reform becomes a mechanism of controlled exposure. The system doesn’t collapse. It tightens. It hardens. It withdraws.
This is not a malfunction. It’s the system doing exactly what it was built to do. VIA James Greenberg

The Inpatient-Only List Is Disappearing, But New Problems Are Appearing

For decades, Medicare maintained a list of procedures that could only be billed as inpatient hospital admissions known as the Inpatient-Only list or IPO. If an orthopedic surgeon performed a complex spinal fusion or a major joint reconstruction, Medicare required an inpatient stay and paid through the IPPS. That process is ending (again).

In the CY 2026 OPPS final rule, CMS began a three-year phase-out of the IPO list, removing 285 mostly musculoskeletal procedures on January 1, 2026, including complex spine and orthopedic surgical codes. CMS proposes to remove an additional 637 procedures in 2027, and to complete the elimination by January 1, 2028. CMS frames this as restoring physician clinical judgment about the appropriate setting of care. The reality is that the decision is more nuanced than purely clinical judgment.

Removal from the inpatient-only list does not automatically place a procedure on the ASC covered procedures list. Those are two distinct lists governed by separate criteria. Some procedures removed from the IPO list were simultaneously added to the ASC covered procedures list in 2026, but that is a separate CMS determination and not automatic. CMS added 547 procedures to the ASC covered procedures list in 2026, but that figure includes procedures moved there by multiple policy pathways. Independent surgeons considering whether IPO removal opens ASC access for a specific procedure need to confirm ASC list eligibility separately.

The more immediate problem for independent physicians is what happens at the hospital and at the payer. On the hospital side, some systems have begun requiring surgeons to obtain inpatient authorization from the payer before the hospital will book the case. If authorization is denied, which is the expected outcome when a payer treats IPO removal as evidence that inpatient admission is never medically necessary, the case cannot be scheduled until the surgeon fights through an appeals process. That delay is an access problem for patients who need the procedure, and the administrative burden lands entirely on the surgeon and their office.

On the payer side, insurers and Medicare Advantage plans treat CMS's removal of a procedure from the IPO list as a policy signal that every such case should be performed outpatient. They issue blanket inpatient denials, require physicians and hospitals to seek case-by-case inpatient authorization, and rarely grant it even when the patient's comorbidities, anesthesia risk, or expected recovery course clearly warrant inpatient monitoring. CMS finalized an exemption from Recovery Audit Contractor patient status review for procedures removed from the IPO list, but that exemption does not bind commercial payers or Medicare Advantage plans.

This is prior authorization by another mechanism. The IPO list gave surgeons a defensible, preauthorized pathway for complex inpatient cases. Its elimination replaces that clarity with a claim-by-claim fight that independent physicians are poorly positioned to win consistently. CMS gave physicians clinical flexibility and handed payers an authorization weapon.

But Medicare Part A and B are also failing, just more quietly, because the damage is hidden on the back end rather than at the point of care.

• Medicare physician reimbursement has fallen roughly 25 to 30 percent in inflation adjusted terms since 2001.
• Cumulative inflation over that period exceeds 75 percent, while the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule has increased less than 15 percent nominally.
• Practice expenses measured by the Medicare Economic Index have consistently outpaced payment updates, leaving many services paid below cost.
• Independent practices increasingly limit new Medicare patients, cut service lines, or sell to hospital systems in response to sustained underpayment.
• Hospital employment of physicians has risen from roughly 25 percent in the early 2000s to over 55 percent today, allowing Medicare losses to be hidden through cross subsidization and facility fees rather than visible access denial.
• Access erosion under traditional Medicare shows up as longer wait times, fewer participating physicians, and geographic care deserts, not denial letters.
• Medicaid pays about 70 percent of Medicare on average, and its chronic access problems show the predictable endpoint when payment stays below cost. Medicare is moving in the same direction, just more slowly.

Health insurance companies delay care to increase profit.

It killed two of my patients.
Their families can't sue.  That's the law.
That's why they keep doing it.  Because there's no reason for them not to.

If your doctor delayed a needed prescription for weeks and you died because of it, your family would rightly sue them into oblivion.

If your insurance company does it?

No accountability, just more profit.

It's federal law.  ERISA preemption.  Health insurance got carved out of normal liability.

That's why Paulina's health insurance killed her.

She was one of the kindest patients I've ever had.  I still think about her.

She had a rare, painful skin disease.  No FDA-approved treatments.  Still kept a great attitude.

There was a drug that worked like magic for patients like her.  Insurance denied it.

Tried everything while we fought to get it for her, but the only things that kept her out of excruciating pain had horrible side effects.

While we appealed, the side effects won.  She died.  The delay didn't just make her suffer longer, it actually killed her.

But it increased profits for her insurance company.

Frank drove hours with his wife to see me.  His little girl was in school.

Severe hand eczema destroying his life.  Constant pain, constant itch, people treating him like he was contagious.

Thought we found the answer - allergic to an ingredient in hand soap.  But avoiding it didn't help.

There's a drug that works great in exactly this situation.  But hands are only 4% of body surface.  Insurance said no need for that drug unless the rash covers 10%.

Threw the kitchen sink at his hands while we fought his insurance.  Kitchen sink didn't help.

Approval came days too late.  His daughter lost her dad.

But more profit for his insurance company.

The economics of drug prior auth are indefensible.

Net savings to the entire US healthcare system: roughly 0.25%.

And that's before you count the dead patients, the hurt patients, the extra care people need while the disease gets worse and the doctor hours pissed away.

In Medicare Advantage, 82% of appealed denials get overturned.  Insurers themselves admit they were wrong four out of five times.

26% of physicians say prior auth has led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care.  8% say it has led to disability, permanent bodily damage, or death.

That's not a fringe number.  One in twelve doctors has watched it kill or cripple someone.

PAs aren't stopping bad prescribing or saving anyone money.

They're grinding down the patients too sick to fight back.  The people working two jobs.  The people who don't have 4 hours a day to spend on the phone.

I pay my employees' health insurance.  Drug costs come out of my pocket too.  Doctors don't prescribe them for fun.

We have skin in the game.  We don't just prescribe expensive drugs willy-nilly.

So, if not to control costs like they claim, why do prior auths exist?

Leverage.

Without PAs, doctors would, lord forbid, just prescribe whatever drug was best for each patient.

Instead, PBMs use PAs to decide which drugs flow and which get buried in paperwork.  Guess which drugs they push?  The ones that generate the most profit for them.

You're shocked, I know.

And they use it as a tool to maximize the profit.  How?  If a pharma company wants easy prior auth, they have to give a huge rebate.

Manufacturers paid PBMs and the payers behind them roughly $170 billion in rebates and fees in 2023.

Wonder why drugs are so expensive?  Because the more expensive the drug, the bigger the rebate, and the PBM keeps a cut of the rebate.

This is the lowest hanging fruit in American healthcare.

There's an easy fix.  Just take away the protection that allows insurance companies to get away with it.

If they delay care the policy said should be covered and it hurts someone, they should be liable.

Make them responsible for hurting people instead of rewarding them.  No complicated policies, just simple 'law of natural consequences'.

We can't bring back Paulina or Frank.

And it's still happening to more people.

Every day.

There's an easy fix.

Just stop protecting the health insurance companies.

By
Noah Tong

October 08, 2025 05:00 AM
Physicians and hospitals are up in arms about new tactics some health insurance companies are using to reduce payments.Under a policy Cigna is rolling out this month, six Current Procedural Terminology Evaluation and Management billing codes are being “downcoded” through an automated process that results in lower reimbursements for services such as office visits and outpatient consultations.Separately, CVS Health subsidiary Aetna is instituting a policy under which some hospital admissions will be automatically approved but reimbursed at lower observation rates.Related: AI, remote monitoring highlighted in AMA’s billing code changesHere’s what you need to know about these new approaches to provider reimbursement.

What is Cigna’s rationale?
Health insurance companies, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and the Health and Human Services Department Office of Inspector General have identified providers “upcoding” claims to generate higher payments as a problem to address.Cigna aims to curtail upcoding by a small group of outliers that affix codes for complex services to claims for basic care, such as treatments for ear infections and sore throats, a Cigna spokesperson said the evaluation and management, or E/M, policy applies to just 1% of in-network providers and providers may appeal for higher payments or apply for exemptions, the Cigna spokesperson said.Cigna Healthcare, the company’s insurance subsidiary, implemented this methodology last Wednesday everywhere except California, where it’s under regulatory review. The company expects the state to allow it to move forward, the spokesperson said.Why do providers object to the Cigna E/M policy?

Provider groups such as the American Medical Association, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the Texas Medical Association and the California Medical Association have expressed concerns that their members will be underpaid, and complained that Cigna is using an opaque process to determine reimbursements and pressuring them to avoid high-level billing codes.Moreover, automatically downcoding claims and instructing providers to appeal adds more red tape and administrative expense to the system, California Medical Association Chief of Staff Janice Rocco wrote in a letter to Peter Welch, president of Cigna Healthcare’s Northern California and the Pacific Northwest operations Aug. 20.“CMA opposes automatic or unwarranted downcoding of claims, and we strongly disagree that simply reducing the E/M [Current Procedural Terminology] code by a single level would result in improved claims accuracy,” Rocco wrote. The practice also conflicts with federal and state policy, she wrote.Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) criticized the policy in a letter sent to Cigna Healthcare Chief Medical Officer Dr. Amy Flaster on Sept. 11. “This new policy will significantly increase administrative burdens and costs for physicians while jeopardizing patient care. I urge you to reverse this decision,” he wrote.The Cigna policy also stoked worry among providers about the growing use of software to automate claims and reimbursements. Cigna doesn’t use artificial intelligence to make final determinations and doesn’t deploy AI for the evaluation and management policy, a spokesperson said.CMS is aware of provider complaints regarding coding practices and AI, and instructs insurers to comply with the Affordable Care Act of 2010, the No Surprises Act, and other federal and state regulations, a spokesperson said.Are other insurers ‘downcoding’ E/M claims?

Aetna, Humana and some Blue Cross and Blue Shield companies have taken similar approaches to E/M claims, provoking ire from providers. Rather than standard denials of payment on a case-by-case basis, insurers increasingly are systematically downcoding them, providers have http://said.Aetna’s program is “highly targeted” and only applies to the 3% of its in-network providers that submit higher-intensity codes than CMS or the AMA recommends, a spokesperson said.The Association for Clinical Oncology asked CMS to scrutinize how UnitedHealth Group subsidiary UnitedHealthcare, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare handle E/M claims in a letter sent Sept. 22.These companies did not respond to requests for comment.What is Aetna’s ‘two-midnight’ policy?
Aetna will implement a “level of severity inpatient payment policy” for hospital services under its Medicare Advantage plans on Nov. 15.Under this twist on the “two-midnight rule,” Aetna will approve admissions for more than one midnight for members who “urgently or emergently” present to hospitals. Although not subject to medical necessity reviews, those services will be reimbursed at the observation rate if Aetna deems they aren’t in accordance with Milliman Care Guidelines for inpatient http://care.Aetna did not respond to a request for comment.Why do providers object to the Aetna Medicare Advantage inpatient policy?

The American Hospital Association, the Federation of American Hospitals and other industry organizations characterized Aetna’s policy as an evasion of the two-midnight standard intended to ensure that hospitals are appropriately paid for inpatient care. Under the two-midnight rule, Medicare Advantage plans and fee-for-service Medicare must pay inpatient rates if patients remain in the hospital for at least two midnights.“This policy could erode the transparency consumers rely on to make informed decisions about their care, undermine important regulatory protections that safeguard patients’ coverage and jeopardize the ability of hospitals to provide high-quality, accessible care to all who need it,” AHA President and CEO Rick Pollack wrote to Aetna President Steve Nelson on Sept. 15.This reimbursement policy violates Aetna’s contracts with providers and will depress reimbursements, the Healthcare Association of New York State, which represents hospitals, wrote in a letter to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz on Aug. 20.The AHA and the Federation also contend that this policy will distort the Medicare Advantage quality scores Aetna receives.“By automatically approving inpatient stays but then depriving full coverage for inpatient stays through severity coverage and partial payments, it appears that Aetna intends to inflate its approval numbers and obfuscate its ultimate inpatient coverage denials, misleading regulators and the public,” Federation of American Hospitals President and CEO Chip Kahn wrote Oz on Sept. 24. “Likewise, by failing to provide notice of adverse organization determinations, Aetna will suppress appeals in ways that directly impact Aetna’s performance on key measures in the Medicare Advantage Star Ratings program.”
